before.name: 2775 BC – 2650 BC: Second Dynasty wars in Ancient Egypt

after.name: 2775 BC: Overview claims Second Dynasty wars; chronology and conflict disputed

r2SourceEvidence.review_note: The century overview offers 2775–2650 without an individual citation. Egyptian Second Dynasty article reports evidence of military conflict under Khasekhemwy, but does not date a continuous war to the overview interval. Seth-Peribsen article debates both division and civil war, including peaceful models. A -2775 slot records that disputed overview claim, not a verified year of fighting, dynastic split or presence of named people. Coordinate/radius remain a broad Egypt gameplay reference.

before.name: c. 2750 BC: Estimated ending of the Cucuteni-Trypillian culture in the region of modern-day Romania, Moldova, and southwestern Ukraine

after.name: c. 2750 BC: One proposed ending for Cucuteni–Trypillia; chronology disputed

r2SourceEvidence.review_note: The century overview says c.2750. The main Cucuteni–Trypillia article begins with c.2950 end and its periodization section lists c.3000; the decline article discusses an end between c.3000 and 2750. None establishes an exact end year, a single cause, or continuity across every location. This -2750 one-year slot is only one disputed dating reference. Coordinate/radius are broad regional game settings.

additions.name: c. 2800–2700 BC: Met Cycladic harp-player sculpture, dating approximate; findspot uncertain

r2SourceEvidence.review_note: The Met dates object 47.100.1 to 2800–2700 BCE and categorizes it as Cycladic, not a precisely dated yearly event. The century page says this Met piece came from Keros, but the Met-linked scholarly article reports it was thought to be from Naxos and discusses contested provenance. The Athens harp-player in Keros article is a different object. Broad Cyclades map point and 100 km radius are regional game references; not the statue findspot, its creation site, or current museum location. No sculptor or player identified. NewsIndex can repeat the interval each year.

additions.name: c. 28th century BC: early Maritime Bell Beaker finds in Tagus region; dating approximate

r2SourceEvidence.review_note: Wikipedia describes early Maritime Bell Beaker examples dated to the 28th century around the Tagus estuary and elsewhere notes c.2750. This interval is a broad reference for archaeological dating, not proof of an exact founding, discovery, continuous pottery production at each year, or entire European distribution in 2800. The map point is a modern Lisbon/estuary regional approximation, not a specific excavation; radius is a game setting and not the ancient distribution. Dates and origin models vary; no associated individuals are asserted.
